catalog_quote: Long vowels are written as double vowels: aa, ii, uu. The distinction between long and short vowels is phonemic: it differentiates between words, as for instance in the following pair of words in Paakantyi: marni fat / maarni corroboree. The first syllable of a word always carries the accent, and vowels in this syllable are more clearly articulated. ... [Hercus & Austin 2004, p. 232:] Malyangapa and Wadikali show phonetic lengthening of single consonants at the beginning of the second syllable following the initial stressed syllable. This feature is shared with Paakantyi to the east, and with Karnic. In Yardliyawara laterals and sporadically also the nasal n have become prestopped in this position

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (ANU E Press, 104 pp., text layer present). extracted text of PDF page 102 (printed p. 92, Appendix 'Transcription of Aboriginal vocabulary', subsection 'Vowels') gives exactly: "The first syllable of a word always carries the accent, and vowels in this syllable are more clearly articulated." — verbatim as reported. The appendix opens (p. 91) "The following consonants are used in Paakantyi and Malyangapa", so the orthography and the accent statement are stated for both Paakantyi and Malyangapa; the same appendix says "All the languages in the general area have three r-sounds", and the book's introduction (p. 4 and pp. 15-16 of the text) identifies the Yarli languages as Malyangapa, W…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word (stated for the orthographies of Paakantyi and Malyangapa in the appendix; corroborated for Malyangapa and Wadikali by Hercus & Austin 2004: 232, which refers to consonant lengthening 'at the beginning of the second syllable following the initial stressed syllable', and for Yardliyawara by prestopping 'in this position').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('the first syllable of a word'); the appendix covers the practical orthography for Paakantyi and Malyangapa vocabulary quoted from Hercus's oral sources; supporting sentence in Hercus & Austin 2004 is about Malyangapa and Wadikali (and, by 'this position', Yardliyawara). Vowel length is phonemic (example given from Paakantyi).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog yarl1236 'Yarli' covers Malyangapa [yga], Wadikali [wdk] and Yardliyawarra [yxl] (all extinct; last Malyangapa speaker d. 1976). The deciding sentence is in Beckett & Hercus 2009's transcription appendix, whose orthography is stated for 'Paakantyi and Malyangapa', so it applies to the Malyangapa variety of Yarli (and to Paakantyi, paak1238, a different subgroup). The corroborating Hercus & Austin 2004 sentence names Malyangapa and Wadikali explicitly and Yardliyawara implicitly ('in this position').
